etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gentilman, morphologically gentle +‎ man, partial calque of Old French gentilhome.

definitions.definition: (chiefly historical) A man of gentle but not noble birth, particularly a man of means (originally ownership of property) who does not work for a living but has no official status in a peerage; (UK law) an armiferous man ranking below a knight.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act II, scene ii:
quote.text: And when their ſcattered armie is ſubdu’d:And you march on their ſlaughtered carkaſſes,Share equally the gold that bought their liues,And liue like Gentlmen in Perſea,  […]

quote.citation: 1593, anonymous author, The Life and Death of Iacke Straw […], Act I:
quote.text: But when Adam delued, and Eue ſpan,VVho was then a Gentleman?

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter VII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “ […]  This is Mr. Churchill, who, as you are aware, is good enough to come to us for his diaconate, and, as we hope, for much longer; and being a gentleman of independent means, he declines to take any payment.” Saying this Walden rubbed his hands together and smiled contentedly.

definitions.definition: Any well-bred, well-mannered, or charming man.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: I corralled the judge, and we started off across the fields, in no very mild state of fear of that gentleman's wife, whose vigilance was seldom relaxed.

quote.citation: 1915, G[eorge] A. Birmingham [pseudonym; James Owen Hannay], chapter I, in Gossamer, New York, N.Y.: George H. Doran Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: As a political system democracy seems to me extraordinarily foolish, […]. My servant is, so far as I am concerned, welcome to as many votes as he can get. […] I do not suppose that it matters much in reality whether laws are made by dukes or cornerboys, but I like, as far as possible, to associate with gentlemen in private life.

quote.citation: 2011, Mike Pappas, Growing Up the Greek Way in the Big Apple, page 103:
quote.text: She wanted to go see a movie called Gigi, which I was not too thrilled about. But being a gentleman, I bit my tongue and said, “Okay.”

definitions.definition: (usually historical, sometimes derogatory) An amateur or dabbler in any field, particularly those of independent means.

quote.citation: 2004, Mary N. Woods, “The First Professional: Benjamin Henry Latrobe”, in Keith L. Eggener, editor, American Architectural History: A Contemporary Reader, electronic edition, Routledge, →ISBN, page 119:
quote.text: Latrobe had extensive dealings with Jefferson, the most prominent gentleman-architect in the United States.

definitions.definition: (cricket) An amateur player, particularly one whose wealth permits him to forego payment.
